title: How does nine months at sea impact your mental health?
description:
After a record 250 consecutive days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln finally docked in Thailand last week. Half of the 5,000 crew members are under 24 years old and they’ve been on board since December, as part of the US-Israel war with Iran.

There have been reports of difficult conditions on board, with food shortages, broken plumbing and concerns about the crew’s morale and mental health, but the US Navy says there haven't been severe problems on board. So how can spending months at sea impact your mental health?

We speak to Dr Harold Kudler, a psychiatrist and former head of mental health policy for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, about the toll this can take. We also hear from Joe Franta, a merchant mariner and YouTuber who documents his experiences working on cargo ships. He shares what it’s like to be at sea for long periods of time.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討長時間在海上生活與服役對海員及軍人心理健康的深遠影響。美國海軍林肯號航空母艦 USS Abraham Lincoln 因中東局勢在海上部署超過 9 個月、連續航行逾 250 天。艦上約 5,000 名官兵中有半數未滿 24 歲，面對空間狹窄、持續噪音、伙食短缺及設施損壞等困境，引發外界對官兵心理健康的關切。前美國退伍軍人事務部心理健康政策負責人兼精神科醫師 Harold Kudler 指出，長期處於高壓、高警備且缺乏明確終點的戰備環境，易引發結合焦慮與憂鬱的病態思鄉病 nostalgia 甚至導致體重大幅減輕與自殺意念；初次部署的年輕官兵也容易因調節不當而精疲力竭。此外，商船海員 Joe Franta 也分享自身經歷，說明連續工作 90 天以上、每日工作 12 小時且每週 7 天無休的封閉生活，會使船隻如同監獄般令人窒息。節目指出，雖然艦上備有心理健康專業人員與同儕支援機制，但官兵常因擔心被視為能力不足而不敢求助，使得心理問題更趨嚴重。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores the psychological toll of extended sea deployments on military personnel and merchant mariners. Prompted by the USS Abraham Lincoln's nine-month deployment—which included a record stretch of over 250 consecutive days at sea—the discussion addresses reports of difficult living conditions, cramped quarters, and declining crew morale. Psychiatrist Dr. Harold Kudler explains how operating under high alert without a clear end date can trigger 'nostalgia' (a form of pathological homesickness combining anxiety and depression), severe weight loss, and suicidal ideation, noting that younger crew members are especially vulnerable to exhaustion. Merchant mariner Joe Franta offers a civilian perspective, describing how relentless 12-hour workdays, sleep deprivation, and extreme isolation after 90 days can turn a ship into a psychological prison. The episode highlights that despite embedded mental health staff and trained peer support on warships, stigma and fear of judgment often stop individuals from seeking help.
